title: The student years
hook: a student lies down in the mud to hold back the water; Hindu tradition calls it the student stage
tomorrow: a hero won his war, then wanted to quit. who talked him out of it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: when it breaks. Every rule breaks sometimes, and now there's a page for that. Today the rule meets something bigger: a whole life, in seasons.
screen: `WHEN IT BREAKS.` → `A WHOLE LIFE, IN SEASONS.`

segments.voice: A first job, and someone older says: enjoy it, these are your learning years. Hindu tradition has a name for that season, brahmacharya, the student stage, and an old story to go with it. A field, and a gap in the bank of a water channel. The teacher, Dhaumya, has sent his student Aruni to stop the leak. Aruni tries to bank it up with earth, and the water won't stop. So he does the only thing left. He lies down in the gap and holds back the water with his own body.
screen: `THESE ARE YOUR LEARNING YEARS.` → `A GAP IN THE BANK.` → `THE WATER PUSHES THROUGH.` → `ARUNI LIES DOWN IN THE GAP.`

segments.voice: Evening comes. The teacher asks his other students: where is Aruni? Then he goes out to the field himself and calls: Aruni of Panchala, where are you? Aruni gets up out of the mud and comes to stand before him. The Mahabharata gives the teacher's answer: because you rose up out of the broken bank, you'll be called Uddalaka, and because you kept my word, all the Vedas will shine in you. Here's the teaching. Hindu tradition names four stages of life, the ashramas, and the first is brahmacharya, the student stage. In the old picture, a student doesn't just take classes. The student lives in the teacher's house, tends the cows and the fire, and learns by serving. Knowledge isn't downloaded; it's handed over, person to person, and the hand-off is earned by showing up. In some Hindu families, a thread ceremony, upanayana, still marks a child's start as a student. The story isn't asking anyone to lie in a ditch. It's showing what the student stage is for: learning to give your whole self to what you were trusted with. Some things can't be learned from a page, only from beside someone, doing the work they gave you. And the stage has an end. One day the student goes home, carrying the teacher's words into a life of his own, and the next season begins.
screen: `ARUNI RISES FROM THE MUD.` · `FOUR STAGES: THE ASHRAMAS.` · `THE STUDENT LEARNS BY SERVING.` · `ONE DAY THE STUDENT GOES HOME.` · then, large: `THE STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Picture the student you were, at the start of your learning years. Say one line to them, quietly, out loud: one thing you've learned since, said kindly, the way a good teacher would say it. Then rest a hand on your chest and stay with that younger self for the rest of the time.
The student years: brahmacharya, the first of the four Hindu stages, learning by serving a teacher. The seasons of life begin here.
Keep this one: the student, and Aruni rising from the mud with the Vedas shining in him. Day 1681, the first season.

Aruni.meaning: the student in the Mahabharata story who held back the water

Uddalaka.meaning: Aruni's new name: the one who rose up from the bank

ashramas.meaning: the four stages of life in Hindu tradition

brahmacharya.meaning: the student stage, the first of the four

upanayana.meaning: the sacred thread ceremony that marks the start of student life

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (the teacher Dhaumya sends Aruni of Panchala to stop a breach in a field's water channel; Aruni lies down in it; called out, he rises and is named Uddalaka and blessed that the Vedas will shine in him)
Laws of Manu 6.87 (the student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the ascetic as four orders)
upanayana, the thread ceremony marking the start of student life
